CALIFORNIA END OF LIFE OPTION ACT (MEDICAL AID-IN-DYING) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D.

ABOUT THIS END OF LIFE OPTION ACT INFORMATION SHEET
This document states facts about California's End of Life Option Act, Health & Safety Code §§ 443–443.22, as it applies to Jordan Alex Lee. The Act creates a statutory pathway under which a terminally ill adult who meets its requirements may request a prescription for a self-administered aid-in-dying drug from an attending physician — here, Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D., if acting in that role for Jordan Alex Lee. This document does not recommend whether Jordan Alex Lee should make a request under the Act, does not constitute the written request form the Act itself requires (Health & Safety Code § 443.11), and is not the attending physician checklist and compliance form referenced in Health & Safety Code § 443.22. Those statutory forms, and the two-physician, two-witness process the Act requires, are completed separately and directly with a participating attending physician. This document instead states what the statute itself says about eligibility, procedure, and legal effect.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: QUALIFIED INDIVIDUAL, TERMINAL DISEASE, AND AID-IN-DYING DRUG
The Act defines a “qualified individual” as an adult who has the capacity to make medical decisions, is a resident of California, and has satisfied the Act's requirements in order to obtain a prescription for a drug to end their life. It defines “terminal disease” as an incurable and irreversible disease that has been medically confirmed and will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months. And it defines “aid-in-dying drug” as a drug determined and prescribed by a physician for a qualified individual, which the qualified individual may choose to self-administer to bring about their death due to a terminal disease.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "“Qualified individual” means an adult who has the capacity to make medical decisions, is a resident of California, and has satisfied the requirements of this part in order to obtain a prescription for a drug to end their life."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(p) (California Legislative Information text), definition of “qualified individual” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.1.)
  "“Terminal disease” means an incurable and irreversible disease that has been medically confirmed and will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(r) (California Legislative Information text), definition of “terminal disease” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.1.)
  "“Aid-in-dying drug” means a drug determined and prescribed by a physician for a qualified individual, which the qualified individual may choose to self-administer to bring about their death due to a terminal disease."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), definition of “aid-in-dying drug” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.1.)
  Known gap: All three quotations below are subsections of a single statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 443.1), not independently authored sources. Section 443.1 defines eighteen separate terms (subdivisions (a) through (r)); this clause reproduces only these three central ones and does not independently verify or reproduce the statute's other defined terms here (for example, “capacity to make medical decisions,” “informed decision,” or “mental health specialist assessment,” each separately defined in the same section).

CONDITIONS THE STATUTE REQUIRES BEFORE A REQUEST MAY BE MADE
By statute, an adult with the capacity to make medical decisions and a terminal disease may request a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug only if several conditions are all satisfied, including that an attending physician has diagnosed a terminal disease, the individual has voluntarily expressed the wish to receive the prescription, the individual is a California resident (established through means such as a California driver's license, voter registration, property ownership or lease, or a recent California tax return), the individual has documented the request in the statutory manner, and the individual has the physical and mental ability to self-administer the aid-in-dying drug. The statute separately states that a person is not disqualified from being a “qualified individual” solely because of age or disability.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "An individual who is an adult with the capacity to make medical decisions and with a terminal disease may make a request to receive a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug if all of the following conditions are satisfied:"
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(a) (California Legislative Information text), introductory conditions for a request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.2.)
  "The individual has the physical and mental ability to self-administer the aid-in-dying drug."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text), physical and mental ability to self-administer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.2.)
  "A person shall not be considered a “qualified individual” under the provisions of this part solely because of age or disability."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(b) (California Legislative Information text), age or disability alone does not disqualify (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.2.)
  Known gap: The quotations below verify only the statute's introductory sentence and the physical/mental self-administration condition (§ 443.2(a) and (a)(5)); this clause's prose summary of the other listed conditions — diagnosis, voluntary expression of the wish, California residency and its four listed proof methods, and statutory documentation — restates but does not separately quote-verify each numbered subpart of § 443.2(a)(1)–(4) here. Section 443.2 also does not itself define “capacity to make medical decisions” (that definition is in a separate subsection of § 443.1, verified in a companion clause of this document) or specify what “physical and mental ability to self-administer” requires beyond this bare statement.

A REQUEST UNDER THE ACT CANNOT BE MADE THROUGH A POWER OF ATTORNEY, ADVANCE DIRECTIVE, OR CONSERVATOR
The statute states that a request for a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug must be made solely and directly by the individual diagnosed with the terminal disease, and cannot be made on that individual's behalf through a power of attorney, an advance health care directive, a conservator, a health care agent, a surrogate, or any other legally recognized health care decisionmaker.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "A request for a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug under this part shall be made solely and directly by the individual diagnosed with the terminal disease and shall not be made on behalf of the patient, including, but not limited to, through a power of attorney, an advance health care directive, a conservator, health care agent, surrogate, or any other legally recognized health care decisionmaker."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(c) (California Legislative Information text), a request cannot be made through a power of attorney, advance directive, conservator, or other decisionmaker (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.2.)
  Known gap: This clause rests on a single statutory subsection (§ 443.2(c)); no independent second source was located restating this exact rule. The subsection states that a request cannot be made through these substitute-decisionmaking mechanisms, but does not itself state a specific legal consequence (for example, invalidity of a request or a particular remedy) if one of these mechanisms is nonetheless used to attempt a request — this document does not assert such a consequence because it was not found stated in this section's text. This document's separate Financial Power of Attorney, Advance Health Care Directive, and adult conservatorship materials describe those instruments generally; none of them independently restates this specific carve-out, so a reader relying on any of those documents together with this one would need to look at this clause for this particular limitation.

THE TWO ORAL REQUESTS AND WRITTEN REQUEST PROCEDURE
By statute, an individual seeking a prescription must submit two oral requests, a minimum of 48 hours apart, and a written request to the attending physician. A valid written request must be signed and dated by the individual seeking the aid-in-dying drug in the presence of two witnesses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "An individual seeking to obtain a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug pursuant to this part shall submit two oral requests, a minimum of 48 hours apart, and a written request to their attending physician."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), two oral requests 48 hours apart plus a written request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.3.)
  "The request shall be signed and dated, in the presence of two witnesses, by the individual seeking the aid-in-dying drug."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), written request must be signed and dated before two witnesses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.3.)
  Known gap: This clause verifies § 443.3(a) and the witness-signing requirement in § 443.3(b)(2); it does not separately quote-verify § 443.3(b)(1) (that the written request must be in the statutory form described in § 443.11) or § 443.3(b)(3) (the witnesses' attestations), which are addressed only in general terms here and, for witness qualifications specifically, in a companion clause of this document. The current 48-hour minimum interval reflects a 2021 amendment (Stats. 2021, Ch. 542 (SB 380), effective January 1, 2022); this document does not address the interval that applied to requests made before that effective date.

LIMITS ON WHO MAY SERVE AS A WITNESS TO THE WRITTEN REQUEST
The statute limits who may witness the signing of the written request: of the two required witnesses, no more than one may be related to the individual by blood, marriage, registered domestic partnership, or adoption, or be entitled to a portion of the individual's estate upon death, and no more than one may own, operate, or be employed at a health care entity where the individual is receiving medical treatment or resides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Only one of the two witnesses at the time the written request is signed may:"
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), no more than one witness may be a relative or estate beneficiary (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.3.)
  "Be related to the qualified individual by blood, marriage, registered domestic partnership, or adoption or be entitled to a portion of the individual’s estate upon death."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), relationship or estate-interest limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.3.)
  "Own, operate, or be employed at a health care entity where the individual is receiving medical treatment or resides."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), health care entity ownership/employment limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.3.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision (§ 443.3(c)), read together with its two numbered items. It does not address the further, separately stated rule in § 443.3(d) that the attending physician, consulting physician, or mental health specialist may not serve as one of the witnesses required under § 443.3(b)(3), nor does it state what legal consequence follows if a written request is witnessed in violation of these limits — no such consequence is stated in this subdivision's text. This witness-eligibility structure is similar in kind to, but is a legally separate statute from, the interested-witness rules that apply to a will under the Probate Code; this document does not assert that the two sets of rules are identical.

EFFECT ON LIFE, HEALTH, AND ANNUITY POLICIES
By statute, the sale, procurement, or issuance of a life, health, or annuity policy — or the rate charged for one — may not be conditioned upon or affected by a person making or rescinding a request for an aid-in-dying drug. Separately, the statute states that a qualified individual's act of self-administering an aid-in-dying drug shall not have an effect upon a life, health, or annuity policy other than that of a natural death from the underlying disease.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The sale, procurement, or issuance of a life, health, or annuity policy, health care service plan contract, or health benefit plan, or the rate charged for a policy or plan contract may not be conditioned upon or affected by a person making or rescinding a request for an aid-in-dying drug."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.13(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), a policy's sale, issuance, or rate cannot be conditioned on a request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.13.)
  "Notwithstanding any other law, a qualified individual’s act of self-administering an aid-in-dying drug shall not have an effect upon a life, health, or annuity policy other than that of a natural death from the underlying disease."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.13(b) (California Legislative Information text), self-administration treated as a natural death from the underlying disease for policy purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.13.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two subdivisions of a single section (§ 443.13(a)(1) and (b)); it does not separately quote-verify subdivision (a)(2) (cross-referencing § 443.18 for the statement that such a death is not suicide) or subdivision (c) (restricting what an insurance carrier may communicate to an individual about aid-in-dying drug availability). No provision addressing how a death certificate itself must record cause of death was located within Health & Safety Code §§ 443–443.22 during this research; this document does not assert a rule on that separate point.

HOW THE ACT CHARACTERIZES A QUALIFYING DEATH, AND LIMITS ON ITS USE IN CONSERVATORSHIP OR ELDER ABUSE PROCEEDINGS
The statute provides that a request by a qualified individual to an attending physician for an aid-in-dying drug, made in good faith compliance with the Act, shall not by itself provide the sole basis for the appointment of a guardian or conservator, and that actions taken in compliance with the Act shall not constitute or provide the basis for any claim of neglect or elder abuse for any purpose of law. Separately, the statute states that nothing in the Act authorizes a physician or any other person to end an individual's life by lethal injection, mercy killing, or active euthanasia, and that actions taken in accordance with the Act do not, for any purpose, constitute suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "A request by a qualified individual to an attending physician to provide an aid-in-dying drug in good faith compliance with the provisions of this part shall not provide the sole basis for the appointment of a guardian or conservator."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.14(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), a request is not the sole basis for a guardian or conservator appointment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.14.)
  "Actions taken in compliance with the provisions of this part shall not constitute or provide the basis for any claim of neglect or elder abuse for any purpose of law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.14(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), compliant actions are not a basis for a neglect or elder abuse claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.14.)
  "Nothing in this part may be construed to authorize a physician or any other person to end an individual’s life by lethal injection, mercy killing, or active euthanasia. Actions taken in accordance with this part shall not, for any purposes, constitute suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.18 (California Legislative Information text), not euthanasia, and not suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.18.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independently numbered statutory sections (§ 443.14, specifically its subdivision (d), and § 443.18), which are genuinely separate sections rather than subsections of one. Section 443.14 contains additional immunity provisions for persons present at self-administration and for health care providers who participate or decline to participate (subdivisions (a) through (c) and (e)), which are not reproduced in this clause. Both quoted provisions are conditioned on compliance “with the provisions of this part” or “in accordance with this part”; this document does not address what follows if the Act's other requirements were not actually met in a given case.

A GOVERNMENTAL ENTITY'S CLAIM AGAINST THE ESTATE FOR COSTS OF A PUBLIC-PLACE DEATH
The statute gives a governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating their life under the Act in a “public place” a claim against that individual's estate to recover those costs and reasonable attorney's fees related to enforcing the claim. “Public place” is separately defined by statute to mean any street, alley, park, public building, place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, or other place open to public view or public access; a health care entity is expressly excluded from that definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Any governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating his or her life pursuant to the provisions of this part in a public place shall have a claim against the estate of the qualified individual to recover those costs and reasonable attorney fees related to enforcing the claim."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.21 (California Legislative Information text), governmental entity's claim against the estate for public-place death costs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.21.)
  "“Public place” means any street, alley, park, public building, any place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, and any other place that is open to the public view, or to which the public has access. “Public place” does not include a health care entity."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(o) (California Legislative Information text), definition of “public place” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=443.1.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two sections (§ 443.21 for the claim itself, and § 443.1(o) for the cross-referenced definition of “public place”). Section 443.21's text does not itself state a limitations period for when the entity must bring this claim, nor does it specify the claim's priority relative to other creditor claims against the estate in a probate proceeding — this document's separate materials on creditor's claims against a decedent's estate describe the general claims process but were not cross-verified here against this specific claim type. The statute does not address costs incurred from a death occurring outside a “public place” as so defined.

LITIGATION HISTORY: THE ACT'S MANNER OF ENACTMENT WAS CHALLENGED, BUT NOT RESOLVED ON THE MERITS BY THIS PUBLISHED DECISION
A published California Court of Appeal decision recounts that the Act was enacted in 2015 during a special legislative session the Governor called for health-care-cost and related purposes, and that a trial court later ruled the Act unconstitutional on the ground that enacting it exceeded the scope of that special session. On the parties' writ petition, the Court of Appeal held that the individual physicians and organization challenging the Act had not adequately alleged standing to do so, and on that basis directed the trial court to vacate its order and judgment — expressly stating that it did not reach the constitutional question of whether the Legislature exceeded its special-session authority in enacting the Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "the Legislature enacted the End of Life Option Act ( Health & Saf. Code, §§ 443 - 443.22 ) (Act), which legalized physician-assisted suicide"
  — People ex rel. Becerra v. Superior Court of Riverside County, 29 Cal. App. 5th 486 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6240060/people-ex-rel-becerra-v-superior-court-of-riverside-cnty/)
  "We will hold that the challengers have not shown that they have standing. Hence, we do not reach the constitutional question."
  — People ex rel. Becerra v. Superior Court of Riverside County, 29 Cal. App. 5th 486 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6240060/people-ex-rel-becerra-v-superior-court-of-riverside-cnty/)
  Known gap: This is the only case-law source in this document; a CourtListener search located this decision without difficulty, and this document's quotes were verified directly against the opinion's text, so no CourtListener quota or access issue is disclosed here. The court's holding was limited to standing — it did not decide, and this document does not assert, whether the Act was validly enacted. (One separate opinion filed in the same case did go on to conclude the Act was constitutionally enacted, but that view was not the basis of the court's disposition and is not treated here as a holding.) This document did not locate or verify any later reported appellate decision resolving the underlying constitutional question on the merits after remand; if the case continued in the trial court after this 2018 decision, that later history is not covered here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This document reflects Jordan Alex Lee's review, as of the date below, of the facts stated above regarding California's End of Life Option Act, Health & Safety Code §§ 443–443.22. It is not a request for an aid-in-dying drug, not the statutory written request form described in Health & Safety Code § 443.11, and not any part of the attending physician checklist and compliance form described in Health & Safety Code § 443.22. Any actual request under the Act is made directly and separately with a participating attending physician — here, Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D., if acting in that role for Jordan Alex Lee — following the statutory procedure described above.

Separately, the statute states that a qualified individual's act of self-administering an aid-in-dying drug shall not have an effect upon a life, health, or annuity policy other than that of a natural death from the underlying disease.

expectedJSON.body: The statute provides that a request by a qualified individual to an attending physician for an aid-in-dying drug, made in good faith compliance with the Act, shall not by itself provide the sole basis for the appointment of a guardian or conservator, and that actions taken in compliance with the Act shall not constitute or provide the basis for any claim of neglect or elder abuse for any purpose of law. Separately, the statute states that nothing in the Act authorizes a physician or any other person to end an individual's life by lethal injection, mercy killing, or active euthanasia, and that actions taken in accordance with the Act do not, for any purpose, constitute suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law.

expectedJSON.body: The statute gives a governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating their life under the Act in a “public place” a claim against that individual's estate to recover those costs and reasonable attorney's fees related to enforcing the claim. “Public place” is separately defined by statute to mean any street, alley, park, public building, place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, or other place open to public view or public access; a health care entity is expressly excluded from that definition.

citations.quote: Any governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating his or her life pursuant to the provisions of this part in a public place shall have a claim against the estate of the qualified individual to recover those costs and reasonable attorney fees related to enforcing the claim.

citations.quote: “Public place” means any street, alley, park, public building, any place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, and any other place that is open to the public view, or to which the public has access. “Public place” does not include a health care entity.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause draws on two sections (§ 443.21 for the claim itself, and § 443.1(o) for the cross-referenced definition of “public place”). Section 443.21's text does not itself state a limitations period for when the entity must bring this claim, nor does it specify the claim's priority relative to other creditor claims against the estate in a probate proceeding — this document's separate materials on creditor's claims against a decedent's estate describe the general claims process but were not cross-verified here against this specific claim type. The statute does not address costs incurred from a death occurring outside a “public place” as so defined.

expectedJSON.body: A published California Court of Appeal decision recounts that the Act was enacted in 2015 during a special legislative session the Governor called for health-care-cost and related purposes, and that a trial court later ruled the Act unconstitutional on the ground that enacting it exceeded the scope of that special session. On the parties' writ petition, the Court of Appeal held that the individual physicians and organization challenging the Act had not adequately alleged standing to do so, and on that basis directed the trial court to vacate its order and judgment — expressly stating that it did not reach the constitutional question of whether the Legislature exceeded its special-session authority in enacting the Act.

citations.case: People ex rel. Becerra v. Superior Court of Riverside County
citations.quote: the Legislature enacted the End of Life Option Act ( Health & Saf. Code, §§ 443 - 443.22 ) (Act), which legalized physician-assisted suicide

citations.case: People ex rel. Becerra v. Superior Court of Riverside County
citations.quote: We will hold that the challengers have not shown that they have standing. Hence, we do not reach the constitutional question.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the only case-law source in this document; a CourtListener search located this decision without difficulty, and this document's quotes were verified directly against the opinion's text, so no CourtListener quota or access issue is disclosed here. The court's holding was limited to standing — it did not decide, and this document does not assert, whether the Act was validly enacted. (One separate opinion filed in the same case did go on to conclude the Act was constitutionally enacted, but that view was not the basis of the court's disposition and is not treated here as a holding.) This document did not locate or verify any later reported appellate decision resolving the underlying constitutional question on the merits after remand; if the case continued in the trial court after this 2018 decision, that later history is not covered here.
